chapters.title: Chapter 2: The New Toolkit of Economic Statecraft

lessons.title: Reading Supply Chain Stress: Shipping Rates, PMI New Orders and Inventory Cycles

children.text: By the time a company's quarterly results confirm a supply chain problem, the problem is usually six to nine months old. Revenue misses and margin compression are lagging indicators, they tell you what already happened. A macro investor who wants to act before the earnings call, not read about it afterward, needs to watch a different set of signals: freight rates, purchasing manager surveys and inventory data. None of these appear on a company's income statement, and all three move well before it does.

body.text: Freight rates, PMI new orders and inventory-to-sales ratios are not obscure economist trivia. They are the earliest publicly available signals that a supply chain is either tightening or breaking, and reading them in sequence tells you roughly how many months you have before that stress reaches company earnings.

children.text: Not all freight indices measure the same thing, and mixing them up is a common mistake. The Baltic Dry Index tracks the cost of shipping dry bulk commodities, iron ore, coal, grain, across a basket of major routes, and moves with raw material demand, especially from China's construction and steel sectors. The Drewry World Container Index and the Freightos Baltic Index instead track containerised freight, the finished and intermediate goods that actually stock retail shelves and factory production lines, and are the more relevant gauge for consumer-facing and manufacturing-linked equities. Chapter 1 already showed one dramatic containerised freight move: Shanghai to Los Angeles spot rates rising from roughly $1,500 to $2,000 per 40-foot container in 2019 to more than $20,000 at the 2021 peak. That spike showed up in freight indices weeks before it showed up in any retailer's cost of goods sold.

body.text: Rising freight rates alone do not tell you whether demand is booming or capacity is broken. Always check the direction of shipping volumes alongside the rate. Rates rising with volumes rising signals genuine demand strength. Rates rising with volumes flat or falling signals a capacity bottleneck, the more concerning pattern for margins downstream.

children.text: The Purchasing Managers' Index surveys factory managers monthly and produces a diffusion index: a reading above 50 signals expansion versus the prior month, below 50 signals contraction. The headline number gets the attention, but the New Orders sub-index is more useful, because new orders received today become production, and eventually revenue, one to two quarters from now. A New Export Orders sub-index, published separately in most major PMI surveys including India's, is the more targeted signal for trade-exposed sectors specifically, since it strips out purely domestic demand.

India's own manufacturing PMI, published by S&P Global, gives a useful real-world range to anchor against. It collapsed to roughly 27.4 in April 2020, the lowest reading in the survey's history at the time, as the national lockdown halted factory activity almost entirely, then recovered into sustained expansion within a year. A reading that low, this far below the 50 threshold, is itself a leading indicator: it told you India's industrial output and, soon after, GDP were about to post historically weak prints, well before either figure was published.

body.label: India Manufacturing PMI, April 2020
body.context: Record low in the survey's history at the time, driven by the national COVID-19 lockdown; a diffusion index reading, where 50 marks the line between expansion and contraction.

children.text: Indicator Three: Inventory-to-Sales Ratios and the Bullwhip Effect

markDefs.definition: The tendency for small, ordinary swings in end-consumer demand to become progressively larger and more volatile as they move upstream through a supply chain, from retailer to wholesaler to manufacturer to raw material supplier, driven by order batching, forecast error and shortage-driven panic ordering.

children.text: An inventory-to-sales ratio simply divides how much unsold stock a business is holding by its recent sales. A rising ratio means stock is building faster than it is being sold, a warning sign that either demand is slowing or a company overordered. The clearest recent illustration is the semiconductor cycle of 2021 to 2023, a textbook case of what supply chain economists call the

: the 2021 chip shortage pushed automakers and electronics makers to double-order chips as a hedge against further shortfalls, which amplified as it moved upstream to chipmakers, who ramped capacity to meet what looked like surging demand. When consumer electronics and PC demand cooled through 2022 as the post-pandemic buying surge faded, all that extra ordering unwound at once. Memory chip prices fell more than 50% through 2022, and both Micron and SK Hynix reported significant operating losses in the following year.

body.title: The Bullwhip Effect: Order Volume Swings Widen Upstream (Illustrative)

children.text: The chart above is illustrative, not real data, but the shape is the point: a modest wobble in end-consumer demand becomes an exaggerated swing by the time it reaches the raw material or component supplier furthest upstream, exactly what played out in the 2021-2023 chip cycle. India's own IT services majors, TCS and Infosys among them, referenced this same destocking dynamic in earnings commentary through 2022 and 2023, as manufacturing and retail clients in the US and Europe cut technology and discretionary spending while working down bloated inventories, a downstream effect of the same bullwhip unwind.

body.title: Calculate the ratio
body.prompt: A manufacturer holds ₹450 crore of inventory and posted ₹300 crore of sales last month. What is its inventory-to-sales ratio, expressed as a multiple (for example, 1.2x)?
body.explanation: ₹450 crore divided by ₹300 crore is 1.5x. If this ratio has been rising for several consecutive months while sales growth is flat or slowing, it is an early warning that either demand is weakening or the company overordered, both of which typically precede a margin or revenue disappointment.

body.caption: A simple screen for rising inventory-to-sales ratios across a watchlist
body.code:
import pandas as pd

# quarterly inventory and sales figures, in INR crore
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "company": ["Alpha Electronics", "Beta Components", "Gamma Devices"],
    "inventory_q1": [320, 210, 180],
    "sales_q1": [260, 240, 200],
    "inventory_q2": [410, 205, 260],
    "sales_q2": [255, 245, 190],
})

df["ratio_q1"] = df["inventory_q1"] / df["sales_q1"]
df["ratio_q2"] = df["inventory_q2"] / df["sales_q2"]
df["ratio_change"] = df["ratio_q2"] - df["ratio_q1"]

# flag companies where the ratio rose by more than 0.15x quarter over quarter
flagged = df[df["ratio_change"] > 0.15]
print(flagged[["company", "ratio_q1", "ratio_q2", "ratio_change"]])

body.title: Order the sequence
body.question: In a typical supply chain stress cycle, which of these signals would you expect to move FIRST?
options: The inventory-to-sales ratio confirming a demand slowdown
GDP growth data showing a manufacturing slowdown
body.explanation: Freight rates are the fastest-moving, most real-time signal of the three, since shipping capacity and demand rebalance almost continuously. PMI new orders follow next, inventory ratios and earnings confirm the stress later, and GDP data, compiled and released with a lag, arrives last of all.

body.title: Reading Supply Chain Stress: Core Terms

cards.definition: An index tracking the cost of shipping dry bulk commodities like iron ore, coal and grain, distinct from containerised freight indices.
The sub-component of the Purchasing Managers' Index measuring new orders received by factories, which leads the headline PMI and industrial output by one to two quarters.
Unsold inventory divided by recent sales; a rising ratio signals demand weakness or overordering, and confirms stress that leading indicators already flagged.
The amplification of ordinary demand swings into progressively larger volatility as they move upstream through a supply chain, illustrated by the 2021-2023 semiconductor cycle.

points: Freight rates, PMI new orders and inventory-to-sales ratios move well before earnings do, and reading them in sequence tells you roughly how many months you have before stress reaches a company's results.

Container freight indices, like the Drewry World Container Index, are the relevant gauge for finished and intermediate goods; the Baltic Dry Index instead tracks bulk raw materials and moves for different reasons.
PMI new orders, and new export orders specifically for trade-exposed sectors, lead the headline PMI and GDP data by one to two quarters.
India's manufacturing PMI fell to roughly 27.4 in April 2020, a real-world example of how a single leading indicator can flag a historic GDP miss before the GDP data itself is even published.
The bullwhip effect explains why modest swings in end-consumer demand can produce dramatic overcapacity or shortage further upstream, as the 2021-2023 semiconductor cycle showed clearly.

Build a simple, repeatable check, such as screening a watchlist for rising inventory-to-sales ratios, rather than waiting for a quarterly result to confirm what leading indicators already suggested months earlier.
